== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High risk (missing-data / sample-loss equivalent in cross-sectional administrative data): Over half of Minas Gerais's 853 municipalities were excluded via unspecified outlier removal (down to n = 574) and listwise deletion of missing SNIS/IBGE fields (down to n = 391 in regressions), with missingness plausibly concentrated in lower-capacity municipalities.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk: Regressions include only the four institutional-capacity factor scores and omit key municipal confounders (GDP/income per capita, urbanization/population density, municipal population size, regional location, and type of service provider such as state utility vs. municipal autarchy), alongside severe simultaneity/reverse causality between per-capita sanitation revenues/expenditures and service coverage.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Municipal legal/policy planning instruments mandated by Federal Law 11.445/2007 (existence of a Plano Municipal de Saneamento Básico [PMSB] and Política Pública de Saneamento Básico [PPSB]) are captured only as self-reported binary dummy variables (1 = yes, 0 = no) in SNIS without verifying statutory enactment quality, regulatory enforcement, contract modality, or actual plan implementation.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk: Both exposure and outcome variables rely heavily on self-reported SNIS municipal/provider declarations (explicitly acknowledged by the authors as potentially correlated with institutional capacity itself), combine asynchronous years (2017 IBGE technical staff vs. 2018 SNIS indicators), and apply Pearson-correlation PCA to binary dummy variables.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Water supply, sewerage, and solid waste collection coverage rates are drawn from standardized SNIS percentage indicators, but rely on unaudited provider self-reports, omit sewage treatment quality/continuity, and restrict sewerage coverage to municipalities served with water without testing sensitivity to missing rural/informal populations.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell regarding pre-specification): No pre-analysis plan or protocol is cited; outlier-trimmed vs. full-sample sensitivity regressions are not reported, although null and counter-hypothesized findings (insignificant political capacity for sewerage and negative association for water supply) are transparently reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High risk: Although the target universe is all municipalities in Minas Gerais (853 municipalities), unspecified boxplot outlier removal reduced the sample to 574 observations and missing self-reported SNIS variables further restricted regression models to 391 municipalities (45.8% of the state's municipalities), creating substantial non-random selection toward municipalities/providers able to report complete SNIS data.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The geographic and temporal scope (municipalities of Minas Gerais using 2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE data) is stated, but the initial number of municipalities retrieved and the operational rules/thresholds used to remove 'a large number of outliers' via boxplots (leaving n = 574) and listwise missing-data exclusions (leaving n = 391 in regressions out of 853 state municipalities) are not specified.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 16-17 / journal pp. 447-448); Section 4 (PDF pp. 19, 22 / journal pp. 450, 453)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional and socioeconomic heterogeneity of Minas Gerais municipalities is described, summary statistics are reported for all variables (Table 2, n = 574), regional spatial patterns of municipal sanitation plans/policies are mapped (Figure 2), and differences across municipal population-size strata are discussed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF p. 10 / journal p. 441); Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 16-17 / journal pp. 447-448); Section 4, Table 2 & Figure 2 (PDF pp. 19-21 / journal pp. 450-452)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Ten municipal institutional-capacity indicators from official secondary databases (SNIS 2018 and IBGE 2017) were combined via Exploratory Factor Analysis (KMO = 0.675, Bartlett p = 0.000, 78.51% variance explained). However, SNIS data are self-reported by service providers (which the authors note may vary with institutional capacity itself), exposure years are asynchronous (2017 vs. 2018), binary dummies were entered into a Pearson correlation PCA rather than polychoric correlations, and PMSB/PPSB dummies capture nominal existence rather than plan quality or implementation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1, Table 1 (PDF pp. 17-18 / journal pp. 448-449); Section 4, Table 3 (PDF p. 22 / journal p. 453); Section 5 (PDF p. 26 / journal p. 457)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Municipalities are legally defined administrative units and variables follow standardized national administrative definitions in IBGE and SNIS, including statutory reference to Law 11.445/2007 for municipal sanitation plans (PMSB) and policies (PPSB).

Although the authors mention municipal population size, population density, socioeconomic conditions, and service-provider scale in the literature review and bivariate ANOVA/chi-square comparisons, they do not explicitly identify socioeconomic, demographic, geographic, or provider-type variables (e.g., state utility vs. municipal provision) as confounders of the relationship between institutional capacity and sanitation coverage.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2 (PDF p. 13 / journal p. 444); Section 4 (PDF pp. 21, 24 / journal pp. 452, 455)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No strategies to control for confounding were implemented in the multivariable analysis. The three OLS regression models (Table 4) include only the four EFA institutional-capacity factor scores as predictors, omitting all socioeconomic, demographic, urbanization, regional, and provider-type controls, and leaving reverse causality/simultaneity between per-capita operating revenues/expenditures and coverage unaddressed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 18-19 / journal pp. 449-450); Section 4, Table 4 (PDF pp. 22-23 / journal pp. 453-454)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Water supply, sewerage, and solid waste collection coverage indicators come from standardized SNIS definitions (Table 1), but SNIS records are self-declared by providers without independent verification—a limitation the authors explicitly note may correlate with provider capacity—and do not capture service continuity or wastewater treatment adequacy.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1, Table 1 (PDF p. 17 / journal p. 448); Section 5 (PDF p. 26 / journal p. 457)

domain_ratings.justification: While heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors and VIF checks were used, the statistical workflow suffers from major flaws: (1) unquantified boxplot outlier deletion and listwise deletion reduced the regression sample to 391 of 853 municipalities without sensitivity checks; (2) Pearson-correlation PCA was applied to binary dummy indicators; (3) unbounded linear OLS was fit to bounded (0-100%), non-normal coverage rates; and (4) per-capita water/sewer revenues and expenditures are mechanically endogenous to water/sewer coverage in a cross-section.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 18-19 / journal pp. 449-450); Section 4, Tables 2-4 (PDF pp. 19, 22-23 / journal pp. 450, 453-454)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This cross-sectional quantitative study examines associations between four factor-analytic dimensions of municipal institutional capacity (financial, political, operational, and technical) and coverage rates of water supply, sewerage, and solid waste collection in Minas Gerais, Brazil, using secondary administrative data from SNIS (2018) and IBGE (2017). Appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies, the study raises High concern for risk of bias (Yes: Q2, Q4; Unclear: Q1, Q3, Q5, Q7; No: Q6, Q8). Major methodological limitations include: (1) severe selection/sample-loss bias, as unspecified boxplot outlier deletion reduced Minas Gerais's 853 municipalities to 574 observations and missing SNIS data further restricted OLS regressions to 391 municipalities (45.8% of the state) without sensitivity analysis, where non-reporting is plausibly linked to weak municipal capacity; (2) complete absence of confounding control in the regressions (omitting municipal GDP/income, population size, urbanization/density, region, and utility provider type); (3) simultaneity/reverse causality, both because per-capita direct operating revenue is mechanically generated by existing billed water/sewer coverage and because low-coverage municipalities may adopt sanitation plans reactively; and (4) reliance on unaudited self-reported SNIS indicators and binary policy dummies entered into Pearson-correlation PCA.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quantitative observational cross-sectional study (exploratory factor analysis and OLS multiple linear regression on municipal secondary administrative data)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, variables, and statistical procedures are reported in Section 3 (Procedimentos metodológicos, PDF pp. 16-19 / journal pp. 447-450, including Table 1). Sample exclusions, descriptive statistics, EFA loadings, and robust OLS regressions are reported in Section 4 (Resultados e discussão, PDF pp. 19-25 / journal pp. 450-456, Tables 2-4 and Figure 2). Self-reporting limitations in SNIS are noted in Section 5 (Considerações finais, PDF p. 26 / journal p. 457).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes a single cross-section of municipal administrative data (2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE) using exploratory factor analysis and multiple linear regression without random assignment, longitudinal follow-up, or a quasi-experimental policy/intervention comparator. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool.
